title: Benefits and Pitfalls of Reinforcement Learning for Language Model Planning: A Theoretical Perspective
claim: Supervised fine-tuning learns spurious co-occurrence structure; adding RL variants reshapes the learned adjacency, with different effects per algorithm.
layout: 4 heatmap panels in a row, left-to-right, shared axes, labels below
description: Four square heatmaps sit side by side, each plotting a 73-by-73 adjacency matrix of graph-node transitions in Blocksworld, with axes ticks from 0 to 70. Panel (a), Edge Frequency, shows the ground-truth edge counts in the SFT data. It has a dark purple background with sparse teal diagonal lines and dots, and a bright yellow bar at the bottom right. Panel (b), SFT, is noisy blue-green with faint diagonal structure and bright yellow dots clustered at the lower right. Panel (c), SFT + PG, is darker and sharper, with a clear bright diagonal and sparser, higher-contrast dots. Panel (d), SFT + Q-Learning, is lighter overall, with blocky bright regions at the right and a strong diagonal. The viridis colormap carries the color. Captions in serif type sit under each panel. The eye goes first to the bright yellow diagonals.
caption: Frequency of edge occurrences in the SFT training data DSFT and the adjacency structures learned by different models. The underlying graph represents transitions between block configurations in Blocksworld (Valmeekam et al., 2023a).
abstract: Recent reinforcement learning (RL) methods have substantially enhanced the planning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet the theoretical basis for their effectiveness remains elusive. In this work, we investigate RL's benefits and limitations through a tractable graph-based abstraction, focusing on policy gradient (PG) and Q-learning methods. Our theoretical analyses reveal that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) may introduce co-occurrence-based spurious solutions, whereas RL achieves correct planning primarily through exploration, underscoring exploration's role in enabling better generalization. However, we also show that PG suffers from diversity collapse, where output diversity decreases during training and persists even after perfect accuracy is attained. By contrast, Q-learning provides two key advantages: off-policy learning and diversity preservation at convergence. We further demonstrate that careful reward design is necessary to prevent Q-value bias in Q-learning. Finally, applying our framework to the real-world planning benchmark Blocksworld, we confirm that these behaviors manifest in practice.
